supplements.citation: Montana DPHHS SNAP 0-3, Introduction; SNAP 103-1, Application Filing/Interview Process; State of Montana SNAP Program Overview (dphhs.mt.gov/hcsd/SNAP/)
supplements.heading: Montana calls its program plainly "SNAP" — no distinctive local brand — but its EBT card has a distinctive state name: the Montana Access Card
supplements.text: Montana DPHHS's own current SNAP manual and consumer page use only the generic federal name "SNAP" (Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program) — this pack found no distinctive Montana-specific program nickname the way California has "CalFresh" or Washington has "Basic Food." Montana's EBT card, however, does carry a distinctive state name: the Montana Access Card. Montana's current self-service application portal is apply.mt.gov. Applicants can also apply by calling the Public Assistance Helpline (1-888-706-1535, which can mail a paper application), by emailing a request for a PDF application to hhssspapplicationcustomersupport@mt.gov, by mail, or in person at a local Office of Public Assistance (OPA). A phone interview is a required step to complete the application. Only a name, address, and signature are required to establish the application filing date; the remainder of the application is completed during the interview (SNAP 103-1). Montana's SNAP program is administered directly and centrally by DPHHS's Human and Community Services Division (HCSD) through local OPAs — a state-administered program with no county-level policy authority, structurally similar to this roster's Nebraska, Connecticut, North Carolina, Ohio, New Jersey, Tennessee, Indiana, Missouri, Maryland, Colorado, South Carolina, Alabama, Louisiana, Kentucky, Oklahoma, Utah, Iowa, Arkansas, Mississippi, Kansas, New Mexico, New Hampshire, Idaho, West Virginia, Hawaii, and Maine packs, and distinct from county-administered states like CA, NY, MN, WI, and VA.

supplements.citation: Montana DPHHS SNAP 001, Gross and Net Income: Standards/Thrifty Food Plan (effective 10/01/2025-09/30/2026); SNAP 304-1, Categorical and Expanded Categorical Eligibility; SNAP 400, Resources Overview; SNAP 403-1, Vehicles
supplements.heading: CORRECTION OF A STALE SECONDARY-SOURCE FIGURE: Montana's own current resource limit is $3,000 (non-elderly/disabled) / $4,500 (elderly/disabled) — NOT the $2,750 figure several secondary sources repeat
supplements.text: Montana DPHHS's own current SNAP 001 (Table of Standards, effective 10/01/2025-09/30/2026) lists three income columns by household size: the 200% FPG Expanded Categorical Eligibility (ECE) gross-income limit ($2,610 for household size 1, rising to $9,026 at size 8), the 130% FPG gross-income limit for non-ECE households ($1,696 at size 1, $5,867 at size 8), and the 100% FPG net-income limit ($1,305 at size 1, $4,513 at size 8). SNAP 304-1 defines Montana's two-tier categorical structure precisely: Traditional Categorical Eligibility (CE, referred to by DPHHS as "CE") covers households in which all members receive or are authorized to receive cash assistance from TANF, TANF Post Employment, Tribal TANF, or SSI, and bypasses both the income and resource tests entirely; Expanded Categorical Eligibility (ECE) covers households in which all members receive or are authorized to receive Montana's TANF Information and Referral Services brochure (a non-cash service), and requires passing only the 200% FPG gross-income test (no net-income test, no resource test). A household that is neither CE nor ECE — including a household with an elderly (60+) or disabled member that fails the 200% FPG ECE gross test — falls back to "regular" eligibility rules: the 130%/100% FPG income tests plus a real, enforced resource limit. This pack fetched Montana DPHHS's own current SNAP 400 (Resources Overview, effective 10/01/2024, current per the 07/01/2026 manual Table of Contents) directly and confirms the operative resource limit is $4,500 for a household with an elderly or disabled member and $3,000 for all other non-CE/non-ECE households. This pack flags explicitly that several secondary sources it found (search-engine-summarized guides, not primary DPHHS text) instead state a $2,750 non-elderly/disabled resource limit — a figure this pack reads as stale, carried over from an earlier COLA cycle (the federal general SNAP resource limit rose from $2,750 to $3,000 effective the FFY2025 cycle nationally), rather than a genuine Montana-specific figure. Vehicle treatment (SNAP 403-1, effective 10/01/2022) follows the federal-baseline exclusion structure rather than a more generous state election: one vehicle with the highest equity value is excluded, plus vehicles used as a home, vehicles whose primary use is to produce income, and certain previously-self-employment vehicles — this pack flags this explicitly as distinct from this roster's New Hampshire pack, which found a more generous "one vehicle per adult household member" exclusion.

supplements.citation: Montana DPHHS SNAP 001, Gross and Net Income Standards; SNAP 304-1, Categorical and Expanded Categorical Eligibility; SNAP 602-4, Shelter Deductions — all effective/current per the 07/01/2026 manual Table of Contents
supplements.heading: CORRECTION OF A WIDELY-REPEATED SECONDARY-SOURCE OVERSIMPLIFICATION: Montana does NOT flatly waive the federal drug-felony SNAP ban — it retains a MODIFIED ban conditioned on compliance with supervision
supplements.text: 21 U.S.C. § 862a(a)(2) sets a federal default: anyone convicted of a state or federal felony for possessing, using, or distributing a controlled substance after 08/22/96 is ineligible for SNAP unless a state opts out or modifies the ban under § 862a(d)(1). This pack found a secondary source (Propel's Montana SNAP guide) stating flatly: "If you're eligible for food stamps, Montana won't disqualify you because of a drug felony." This pack fetched Montana DPHHS's own current SNAP manual text directly — appearing consistently, word-for-word, in three separate sections (SNAP 001's gross-income-test exceptions list, SNAP 304-1's CE/ECE-exclusion list, and SNAP 602-4's shelter-deduction carve-out language) — and found the actual rule is more precise and narrower than the secondary source's framing: an individual is disqualified if convicted after 08/22/96 of a federal or state felony for possession, use, or distribution of illegal drugs "AND not complying with conditions of supervision." This pack reads this as a genuine MODIFIED ban, not a full opt-out: an individual who is complying with the terms of their probation or parole (which commonly, though not necessarily always, include a treatment-program condition) is NOT disqualified, but an individual who is convicted and is NOT in compliance with supervision conditions genuinely IS disqualified from SNAP on this basis alone. This pack treats the secondary source's "won't disqualify you" framing as an overclaim that omits the supervision-compliance condition entirely, and flags this explicitly as a correction rather than a confirmation — Montana's actual policy retains a real, live, currently-enforced disqualification pathway, distinct from this roster's New Hampshire and Maine packs, which each confirmed a genuine FULL opt-out via their own states' primary-source 1990s implementing directives/statutes. This pack independently confirmed no standalone Montana Code Annotated statute addressing this specific condition exists in Title 53, Chapter 2, Part 9 (Food Stamp Program) — the modifier is implemented through DPHHS policy/administrative rule rather than legislative opt-out, which this pack flags as a structural detail worth distinguishing from a legislatively-enacted opt-out like New Hampshire's HB 722-FN. This is separate from Montana's fleeing-felon/probation-violation disqualification (a distinct CE/ECE-exclusion category listed alongside the drug-felony provision) and from the SNAP 705-1 work-registration disqualification (voluntary-quit/hour-reduction penalty periods), neither of which this pack conflates with the drug-felony-conviction rule.

supplements.citation: Montana DPHHS SNAP 602-2, Deductions (Earned, Standard, Dependent Care, Child Support); SNAP 602-3, Deductions (Medical); SNAP 602-4, Shelter Deductions — Standard Utility Allowance $799, Limited Utility Allowance $267, One Utility Allowance $116, Telephone Allowance $34; Standard Deduction $209 (household sizes 1-3), $223 (4), $261 (5), $299 (6+); Medical Expense Deduction (actual expense, $35/month threshold, no flat shortcut)
supplements.heading: Montana's utility-allowance structure follows the conventional SUA/LUA/OUA/Telephone four-tier, count-based split — a $799 Standard Utility Allowance for households with heating/cooling costs
supplements.text: Montana's Standard Deduction (per DHHS's current SNAP 602-2) is $209 for household sizes 1 through 3, $223 for size 4, $261 for size 5, and $299 for size 6 or more — matching the current national FFY2026 figures this roster's other states have each independently confirmed. Montana's utility-allowance structure (SNAP 602-4, effective 10/01/2025) is a conventional four-tier, count-based split rather than the type-based split this roster's New Hampshire pack found: the Standard Utility Allowance (SUA) is $799/month for households incurring heating or cooling expenses separately from rent/mortgage, or billed individually by a landlord for heating/cooling, or (for elderly/disabled households) receiving more than $20/year in LIHEAP or similar energy assistance; the Limited Utility Allowance (LUA) is $267/month for households not entitled to the SUA that incur at least two non-heating/cooling utilities (electricity, water, sewer, garbage, telephone); the One Utility Allowance (OUA) is $116/month for households incurring only one non-heating/cooling utility; and a standalone Telephone Allowance is $34/month for households incurring only telephone costs. This pack flags that Montana's LIHEAP-triggered automatic-SUA-eligibility pathway is explicitly restricted to elderly/disabled households only (a household without an elderly/disabled member cannot use a LIHEAP payment alone to trigger SUA eligibility, though it can still qualify via directly-billed or separately-metered heating/cooling costs) — the same LIHEAP-trigger restriction this roster's New Hampshire pack found, worth naming since not every state built in this roster restricts the trigger this way. Montana's Medical Expense Deduction (SNAP 602-3) is an ACTUAL-EXPENSE deduction with NO flat shortcut: elderly (60+) or disabled household members can deduct total medical expenses exceeding $35/month, verified at every application and recertification — this pack flags this explicitly as placing Montana with this roster's Nebraska, Connecticut, Maryland, and Indiana packs' actual-expense-only camp, in contrast to states (including this roster's New Hampshire, Kentucky, Louisiana, South Carolina, Missouri, Colorado, and Alabama packs) that use a flat-dollar shortcut instead. Montana's homeless standard shelter deduction and its excess-shelter-deduction annual cap are both described in SNAP 602-4 as being "updated each year by 09/01," but this pack did NOT find the current specific dollar figures for either published anywhere in the SNAP 602-4 section text itself — this pack flags both figures explicitly as an unconfirmed gap in freshness.json rather than guessing or fabricating a number, and recommends checking DPHHS's own income-standards materials or contacting a local Office of Public Assistance directly before stating either figure with confidence.

supplements.citation: Montana DPHHS SNAP 801-1, ABAWD Countable Months/Exemptions (current, post-11/1/2025 text, effective 10/01/2025); SNAP 802-1, ABAWD Geographic Waiver (effective 11/01/2025)
supplements.heading: Montana currently has NO approved ABAWD geographic waivers anywhere in the state — confirmed directly and unambiguously by DPHHS's own current policy text
supplements.text: An able-bodied adult without dependents (ABAWD) is limited to three countable months of SNAP within a three-year period absent 20 hours/week (averaged monthly) of a qualifying work activity or an exemption. This pack fetched Montana DPHHS's own current SNAP 801-1 (ABAWD Countable Months/Exemptions, effective 10/01/2025) directly and confirms the current, post-11/1/2025 OBBBA exemption list: age 17 or younger (the month after the 18th birthday begins the countable clock); age 65 or older (SNAP 801-1's own text explicitly states this threshold was RAISED from 55, effective 11/01/2025 — the pre-OBBBA exemption age was 55+, the current exemption age is 65+, consistent with the OBBBA nationwide ABAWD-age-scope expansion from 18-54 to 18-64 this roster has documented in other 2025-2026-built packs); physically or mentally unfit for employment; parent (or resident) of a household member under age 14 (narrowed from under 18); pregnancy with medical documentation; and being an Indian/Urban Indian/California Indian eligible for Indian Health Services (IHS) — a newly-added exemption category consistent with the federal OBBBA rollout. This pack flags explicitly that Montana's GENERAL (non-ABAWD) work registration requirement covers a separate, wider age band — able-bodied household members age 16 through 59 must register for work under Montana's own consumer-facing SNAP page — and cautions against conflating the two distinct age ranges: the 16-59 general work-registration band and the 18-64 ABAWD time-limit band serve different purposes and carry different consequences. This pack's most consequential finding in this supplement is the CLEANEST, most directly-confirmed waiver-status statement this roster has found for any state: Montana DPHHS's own SNAP 802-1 (ABAWD Geographic Waiver, effective 11/01/2025) states in full: "As of 11/01/2025, there are no areas within Montana with approved ABAWD geographic waivers" — a plain, unambiguous, directly-fetched primary-source statement, rather than an inference this pack had to draw from a waiver index's absence of a current entry (the method this roster's New Hampshire and Maine packs each had to rely on).

supplements.citation: USDA FNS SNAP Restaurant Meals Program — nine currently participating states (AZ, CA, IL, MD, MA, MI, NY, RI, VA), Montana absent (WebSearch corroboration); Montana DPHHS SNAP 0-3, Introduction
supplements.heading: Montana does NOT operate a Restaurant Meals Program — but DOES carry the standard narrower federal congregate/meal-delivery-service provision for elderly and SSI households
supplements.text: The Restaurant Meals Program (RMP) is a state OPTION under 7 CFR § 274.7(g) letting elderly (60+), disabled, and homeless SNAP recipients buy prepared, hot meals from authorized restaurants with EBT year-round; as of this pack's research, nine states currently participate nationally (Arizona, California, Illinois, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, New York, Rhode Island, and Virginia), and Montana is not among them (WebSearch corroboration — this pack's direct WebFetch attempt against fns.usda.gov's own RMP page timed out and was not independently confirmed at the primary source; flagged in freshness.json). This pack fetched Montana DPHHS's own SNAP 0-3 (Introduction) directly, which states plainly that alcoholic beverages, household products, cigarettes, hot foods ready to eat, and pet food cannot be purchased with SNAP benefits — the standard federal restriction — but ALSO states: "A limited number of participants who meet specific eligibility and residence criteria may use their SNAP benefits to buy prepared meals e.g. authorized meal delivery service, authorized communal dining facility for elderly or SSI households, etc." This pack reads this precisely as the standard, much narrower federal congregate/meal-delivery-service provision (available in every state, not a state-option RMP) rather than a state-elected Restaurant Meals Program, and flags the distinction explicitly so the two are not conflated: an applicant asking whether they can use SNAP at an ordinary restaurant in Montana should be told plainly no, while an elderly or SSI-recipient applicant asking about an authorized meal-delivery service or communal dining facility has a narrower, federally-standard pathway that is NOT restaurant dining.

supplements.citation: Montana DPHHS SNAP 1502-1, Recertification — 24 months for all-elderly/disabled no-earned-income households; 12 months for Simplified Reporting households; up to 24 months for change-reporting households with a required 12-month contact
supplements.heading: Montana's certification periods follow the conventional national pattern — 12 months standard, 24 months for elderly/disabled no-earned-income households
supplements.text: Montana DPHHS's own current SNAP 1502-1 (Recertification) states that households in which all members are elderly or disabled with no earned income are certified for 24 months, while all other households are certified for 12 months (Simplified Reporting) — a more conventional national-norm structure than this roster's New Hampshire pack found (6-month standard, 36-month ESAP). Change-reporting households (a narrower category than Simplified Reporting) can be certified for up to 24 months, but must have at least one contact with DPHHS every 12 months regardless. A recertification interview is required at least once every 12 months for Simplified Reporting households and at least once every 24 months for change-reporting households. If a change-reporting household member becomes disqualified and the household's certification period is more than 12 months away, the recertification date must be shortened to month 12 — a specific administrative rule this pack found worth flagging, since it means a household's certification length can shorten mid-period based on a change in household composition, not just at the household's own request. A household receives a Redetermination/Recertification Report form and a Notice of Expiration (NOE) by the 15th of the month before its recertification month, consistent with the standard federal 7 CFR 273.14(a)(2) notice requirement.
